pages.text: Ohm's law works for AC just as it does for DC, once the opposition is the impedance Z: `I = V ÷ Z`. The supply voltage V is drawn along the real axis, at 0°, and every other angle is measured from it.

pages.name: Dividing by Z
pages.task: An 8 Ω resistor and a 6 Ω coil, `Z = 8 + j6`, are in series on 230 V. What current flows?
pages.why: Z is `8 + j6 = 10∠36.87° Ω`. Dividing divides the lengths, `230 ÷ 10 = 23` A, and takes the angles away, `0° − 36.87° = −36.87°`. So `I = 23∠−36.87° A`: 23 A on a clamp meter, lagging the voltage by Z's angle.

pages.name: Measured from what?
pages.task: The current is `I = 23∠−36.87° A`. What is its −36.87° measured from?
pages.why: A single wave's angle depends on when you start the clock; only the gap between two waves means anything. We chose the supply voltage as the zero and drew it at 0°, so I's −36.87° says it is 36.87° behind V. Start the clock 30° later and V reads `230∠30°` and I `23∠−6.87°`: both angles change, but the gap is still 36.87°, Z's angle.

pages.name: A capacitor instead
pages.task: Swap the coil for a capacitor of 6 Ω, so `Z = 8 − j6`. What current flows from the 230 V supply now?
pages.why: `8 − j6` is `10∠−36.87° Ω`: the same length as before, pointing down. So `I = 230∠0° ÷ 10∠−36.87° = 23∠36.87° A`. The +36.87° is measured from the supply voltage: the current leads V by 36.87°, where the coil made it lag.

pages.text: In series one current flows through every part, so each part's voltage is that current times the part's own impedance. The two voltages add as arrows, tip to tail, back to V.

pages.name: Two meter readings
pages.task: In that circuit a meter reads 184 V across the resistor and 138 V across the coil. What voltage is the supply giving?
pages.why: The resistor's 184 V lies along the current and the coil's 138 V stands a quarter turn ahead of it, so they add as arrows, tip to tail. They meet at a right angle, so the voltage triangle you already know gives the supply: `√(184² + 138²) = √52900 = 230` V. In parts it checks: `(147.2 − j110.4) + (82.8 + j110.4) = 230 + j0`.

pages.text: Side by side, each branch has the whole supply across it, so each branch current is V divided by that branch's own impedance. The branch currents add to make the supply current, as with DC, but as arrows.

pages.name: Two 23 A branches
pages.task: Side by side on 230 V, the coil branch draws 23 A and a −j10 Ω capacitor draws 23 A. What current does the supply give?
pages.why: Add by parts: `(18.4 − j13.8) + j23 = 18.4 + j9.2`. Its length is `√(338.56 + 84.64) = 20.57` A, at `tan⁻¹(9.2 ÷ 18.4) = 26.57°`. The capacitor's j23 cancels the coil's −j13.8 and leaves j9.2 over, while the 18.4 A real part is untouched.

pages.text: Product over sum, the reciprocal rule worked out for two branches, works here just as you use it for two resistors. It turns the pair into one impedance Z, which gives the same supply current.

pages.name: A capacitor in series
pages.task: To finish, three mixed puzzles: choose the form first. A 6 Ω resistor and a capacitor of 8 Ω are in series on 230 V. How far is the current from the supply voltage, and which way?
pages.why: Adding is a job for parts: the capacitor gives −j8, so `Z = 6 − j8`. An angle is a job for length and angle: `Z = 10∠−53.13° Ω`, pointing down. Taking its angle away, `0° − (−53.13°) = +53.13°`: the current leads the supply voltage by 53.13°.

pages.name: Two equal branches
pages.task: Choose the form first. Two equal branches, each an 8 Ω resistor with a 6 Ω coil, `8 + j6 = 10∠36.87° Ω`, are side by side on 230 V. What current does the supply give?
pages.why: Product over sum, each job in its own form. The bottom is a sum, so add by parts: `16 + j12 = 20∠36.87°`. The top is a product, so multiply by length and angle: `10∠36.87° × 10∠36.87° = 100∠73.74°`. Dividing gives `5∠36.87° Ω`, so `I = 230 ÷ 5 = 46` A at −36.87°. All in parts works too, as in the first lessons: `(8 + j6)² = 64 + j96 + j²36 = 28 + j96`, because `j × j = −1`, and times the bottom's conjugate `16 − j12`, top and bottom, `(1600 + j1200) ÷ 400 = 4 + j3`, the same 5∠36.87°. By branches: each draws `23∠−36.87° A`, pointing the same way, so they add straight, to 46 A.

pages.name: From the current to Z
pages.task: Choose the form first. A load on 230 V draws `11.5∠−36.87° A`. What is its impedance Z, in parts?
pages.why: `V = IZ`, so `Z = V ÷ I`, a division, which is a job for length and angle: `230∠0° ÷ 11.5∠−36.87° = 20∠36.87° Ω`. Then change form for the answer in parts: `R = 20 cos 36.87° = 16` and `X = 20 sin 36.87° = 12`. So `Z = 16 + j12`: 16 Ω of resistance with a coil's 12 Ω.
